text: A New Hybrid Solid/Solvating Sulfur Conversion for Energy-Dense Lithium-Sulfur Batteries Xiaoyu Jin, Xiaoqun Qi, Fengyi Yang, Han Zhou, Ruining Jiang, Dan Yang, Zhou Fang, Fei Zhou, Jie Ji, Zhenglu Zhu, Lixia Yuan*, Yunhui Huang , and Long Qie* 1.

Introduction Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery based on the conversion chemistry of 2Li + S →Li2S delivers an ultrahigh theoretical energy density of 2600 Wh kg1.[1–7] However, in practical terms, its available energy density is low because the operation of Li-S batteries in the mainstream dioxolane/dimethoxyethane (DOL/DME) electrolyte requires a high electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio (usually >5 μL mg1).[8–12] DOL and DME with high donor numbers show high dissolution of the Li polysulfides (LPSs); therefore, the 1M ether electrolyte participates in the “dissolution-precipitation” conversion process at the cathode side and converts to catholyte after dissolving LPSs.[13,14] Under lean-etherelectrolyte conditions, our previous work revealed that S cathodes suffer from sluggish conversion kinetics caused by significantly decreased Li+ conductivity and deteriorated wettability of the high-LPSs-ratio catholyte.[15] In addition to low gravimetric energy density, the volumetric energy density of Li-S batteries is largely limited by the demand for high-porosity (>70%) S cathodes.[16] A dense S cathode fails to work in conventional ether electrolytes because it undergoes a locally low E/S ratio with a decreased electrolyte uptake in the cathode structure.

Catalytic cathodes and mediation additives have been extensively exploited to improve the conversion kinetics under low E/S ratios, but their effects are limited to a certain extent.[17–24] Sparingly solvating electrolytes are promising candidates to decrease the E/S ratio by fundamentally altering the conversion pathway.

Sparingly solvating electrolytes were developed by increasing Li salt to an extent where the electrolyte mainly consists of Li salt-solvent coordination with little free solvent.[25] This unique electrolyte structure can effectively suppress the dissolution of LPSs and consequently drives a solid conversion process, which is expected to be less dependent on electrolyte amount in comparison to the “dissolution-precipitation” process in solvating electrolytes.[26] A series of acetonitrile (AN)-,[27–29] ether-,[30–32] carbonate-,[33,34] and sulfolane-based sparingly solvating electrolytes have been developed.[35] Among them, AN-based ones successfully enable Li-S batteries to operate under the lowest E/S ratio of 1 μL mg1 as previously being demonstrated.[15,29] However, the use of sparingly solvating electrolytes is critically challenged by sluggish S redox chemistry due to the solid conversion pathway and the very low Li+ conductivity of the electrolyte.

Herein, a new hybrid solid/solvating conversion pathway, that is, S converting to both solid and solvated LPSs, is achieved by a moderately solvating electrolyte, which combines lean-electrolyte operation as in sparingly solvating electrolytes and fast conversion kinetics as in solvating electrolytes.

The moderately solvating electrolyte is formulated by methoxyacetonitrile (MAN) since MAN possesses a high relative permittivity (21) that contributes to a high Li+ conductivity of 11.7 mS cm1 for 1M lithium bis(trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) in MAN, along with a low donor number (14.6 kcal mol1) that brings about a decreased solubility to LPSs (1/6 of that in DOL/DME).

DOI: 10.1002/eem2.70139 To boost the practical energy density of lithium-sulfur batteries, replacing conventional solvating electrolytes with sparingly solvating ones has shown promise by enabling solid-state sulfur conversion and reducing electrolyte consumption.
However, this approach often compromises sulfur redox kinetics.
This study reports a new sulfur conversion pathway distinct from both traditional solvated and sparingly solvated mechanisms.
Specifically, sulfur is converted into a mixture of solid and solvated lithium polysulfides (LPSs).

Such a hybrid solid/solvating conversion pathway is achieved using a newly formulated moderately solvating electrolyte, accomplishing both lean-electrolyte operation and fast conversion kinetics for lithium-sulfur batteries.

Methoxyacetonitrile (MAN) is selected as the solvent to formulate the moderately solvating electrolyte due to its high relative permittivity (21) that contributes to a high Li+ conductivity (11.7 mS cm1 for 1M lithium bis(trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide in MAN) and low donor number (14.6 kcal mol1) that reduces the solubility to LPSs to 1/6 of that in mainstream solvating electrolytes.

The as-formulated MAN electrolyte enables sulfur cathodes to operate at a low electrolyte-to-sulfur ratio of 2 μL mg1 and a low cathode porosity of 52%, displaying excellent prospects for boosting both gravimetric and volumetric energy density.

The hybrid solid/solvating conversion pathway contributes to well-maintained high ionic conductivity and good wettability of the electrolyte during the conversion process, successfully circumventing the dependence of battery performance on electrolyte dosage.
The 1M MAN electrolyte enables S cathodes to run at a low E/S ratio of 2 μL mg1 and a low cathode porosity of 52%. 2.

Results and Discussion S cathodes undergo different conversion pathways in different electrolytes.[36–38] In highly solvating electrolytes, for example, 1M LiTFSI in DOL/DME, S cathodes perform the well-known “dissolution-precipitation” conversion pathway,[39] of which the “dissolution” step is solid S converting to solvated LPSs as shown in Figure 1.
This conversion mechanism offers fast kinetics because the solvated LPSs function as mediators to promote redox reactions.

However, the “dissolution” process fundamentally requires a high E/S ratio (usually >5 μL mg1) to fully dissolve LPSs intermediates, leading to a significant reduction in the overall energy density of Li-S batteries as shown in Figure S1, Supporting Information.
With sparingly solvating electrolytes, S cathodes almost perform a solid conversion process.
Leveraging this mechanism, the E/S ratio can be reduced to extremely low levels, thereby significantly enhancing the energy density of the system.
The changes in mass distribution and the improvement in energy density resulting from the reduced E/S ratio are illustrated in Figure S2, Supporting Information.
The specific mass parameters of each component and the corresponding energy densities are presented in Tables S1 and S2, Supporting Information, respectively.
But Li-S batteries suffer from sluggish conversion kinetics in sparingly solvating electrolytes, which can be attributed to two aspects.
One is that the conversion process from solid S to solid LPSs without the mediation of solvated LPSs is kinetically slow.

The other is that sparingly solvating electrolytes commonly have low Li+ conductivity,[30,40–41] for example, 0.27 mS cm1 for a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte (G20.8LiTFSI, the molar ratio of G2 to LiTFSI is 0.8:1, diluted by 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropylether), in comparison with a high Li+ conductivity of 12.6 mS cm1 for the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte as shown in Figure S3, Supporting Information.

The sluggish kinetics in sparingly solvating electrolytes leads to unsatisfying cyclability and poor rate performance.[42] Besides, sparingly solvating electrolytes are costly due to their high content Li salts, which makes them difficult to be used in large scale.
Disappointingly, the electrolytes designation for Li-S batteries always follows the above two principles: highly solvating electrolytes and sparingly solvating electrolytes.
Although Li-S batteries based on these electrolytes have made great progress, the development is limited to the laboratory level and is far from being practical.

Under this circumstance, a moderately solvating electrolyte that has a moderate solvating ability, lower than that in highly solvating electrolytes but higher than that in sparingly solvating electrolytes, toward LiPSs is immediately needed to induce new hybrid solid/solvating sulfur conversion, and thus guarantee the operation of Li-S batteries under lean-electrolyte condition with fast conversion kinetics.
Here, MAN is selected to formulate the moderately solvating electrolyte.

Among common aprotic solvents, nitriles have distinguished characters, with high relative permittivity that offers high Li+ conductivity, and with low donor number that brings about low dissolution to LPSs.

A typical example is acetonitrile (AN); however, it has a poor reductive stability and severely reacts with Li metal (Figure S4, Supporting Information).[43] In comparison with AN, the introduction of methoxy for MAN reduces the polarization degree (Figure 2a), which lowers the ability of MAN to acquire electrons and thus contributes to enhanced compatibility with Li metal, as demonstrated by the immersion tests (Figure S4, Supporting Information).
The basic properties of MAN are further compared with DOL and DME.
MAN has a decent relative permittivity of 21 that is beneficial to Li+ conductivity,[44] in comparison to DOL (6.8) and DME (7.2) (Figure 2b).
Figure 2c exhibits MAN-based electrolytes perform high Li+ conductivity comparable to the value of DOL/DME-based electrolytes at different concentrations.
In this work, we applied the 1M MAN electrolyte with a high Li+ conductivity of 11.7 mS cm1 into Li-S batteries, with the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte as the baseline.
Besides, MAN has a lower donor number of 14.6 than DOL (21.2) and DME (21.0), which contributes to lower dissolution to LPSs (Figure 2b).

To demonstrate the moderately solvating character of MAN, we prepared Li2S6-saturated DOL/DME and MAN solutions by stoichiometrically reacting Li2S and S (detailed preparation in Experimental Section).
As shown in Figure 2d, The Li2S6-saturated MAN shows a light brown color in contrast to a dark black color for the Li2S6-saturated DOL/DME, indicating a lower LPSs solubility in MAN solution.

The Li2S6 solubility was measured via a precipitation method previously reported by Zhang et al.[45] Benefited from the low DN, MAN shows a solubility to LPSs of 3 mol L1 based on S1/3 (Figure 2d), which is only 1/6 of that in DOL/DME.
Subsequently, we prepared Li2S6-saturated electrolytes to simulate the property evolution of catholyte under lean electrolyte conditions.
The 1M DOL/DME electrolyte shows a significant decrease of Li+ conductivity from 12.7 to 5.7 mS cm1 with saturated Li2S6 (Figure 2e).
In contrast, the 1M MAN electrolyte maintains a high conductivity of 11.7 mS cm1 with saturated Li2S6.
The contact angle of electrolytes and Li2S6-saturated electrolytes was tested to evaluate the wettability, as shown in Figure 2f.
The pristine 1M DOL/DME electrolyte displays a low contact angle of 28° on S cathodes, but it shows a significant increase to 85° with saturated Li2S6, indicating wettability deterioration Figure 1.

By comparison, the pristine 1M MAN electrolyte and the Li2S6-saturated one exhibit the same low contact angle of 26°.
The reduced LPSs solubility mitigates the deterioration of electrolyte solvation structure and physical properties caused by LPSs dissolution during discharge.

Coupled with MAN’s inherent high relative permittivity, the 1M MAN electrolyte maintains its fast Li+ conductivity and good wettability during S conversion, thereby establishing the foundation for leanelectrolyte operation.
The MAN electrolyte brings about new S conversion behaviors.

The electrochemical performance of Li-S batteries in the moderately solvating MAN electrolyte is compared with that in the mainstream 1M DOL/DME electrolyte (an example of highly solvating electrolytes) and the G20.8LiTFSI electrolyte (an example of sparingly solvating electrolytes).

The Li-S battery shows a typical two-plateau discharge profile in the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte corresponding to the “dissolutionprecipitation” process, and shows a one-plateau discharge profile in the G20.8LiTFSI electrolyte corresponding to the solid conversion process.

Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) test was performed to confirm the anodic oxidation stability of the solution (Figure S6, Supporting Information) and the onset potential of oxidative decomposition close to 4.0 V (vs Li/Li+) far exceeding the charging cut-off voltage (2.8 V) of Li-S batteries.

When applying the 1M MAN electrolyte, the Li-S battery also displays a two-plateau discharge profile (Figure 3a), but the first plateau shows a lower voltage of 2.23 V than that in the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte of 2.28 V, and the second plateau shows a higher voltage of 2.14 V in comparison to 2.09 V for the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte.

CV curves (Figure 3b) show similar results, with two reduction peaks at 2.19 and 2.06 V for the 1M MAN electrolyte, in comparison to two reduction peaks at 2.28 and 1.99 V for the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte, and one reduction peak at 1.52 V for the G20.8LiTFSI electrolyte.
The electrochemical behavior of S in the 1M MAN electrolyte is thermodynamically and kinetically different from that in 1M DOL/DME and G20.8LiTFSI electrolytes.
Galvanostatic intermittent titration techniques (GITT) were performed to compare equilibrium states of Li-S batteries with different electrolytes.

As shown in Figure 3c, the S conversion process with the 1M MAN electrolyte is thermodynamically different from that with 1M DOL/DME and G20.8LiTFSI electrolytes, indicated by diverse equilibrium voltage.
Besides, GITT profiles demonstrate the 1M MAN electrolyte provides the fastest conversion kinetics among the three electrolytes.
The Li-S battery with the G20.8LiTFSI electrolyte unsurprisingly shows high overpotentials during the whole discharge process, owing to the slow solid conversion pathway and low Li+ conductivity.
As for the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte, it is widely accepted to afford fast redox Li-S chemistry with the mediation effect of solvated LPSs, and the corresponding GITT profile shows low overpotential.
However, when applying the 1M MAN electrolyte, the overpotential is even lower than the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte at the first discharge plateau, indicating more favorable conversion dynamics.
Rate performance (Figure 3d) is further compared for the three electrolytes.
The G20.8LiTFSI electrolyte offers the poorest rate performance with only 85 mAh g1 at 1C.
The Li-S battery with the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte shows better tolerance to high discharge current, but the discharge capacity significantly decreases to 187 mAh g1 at a high C rate of 5C.
In contrast, the 1M MAN electrolyte provides the best rate performance with 416 mAh g1 remaining at 5C.
The above results demonstrate the 1M MAN electrolyte alters the conversion mechanism of S cathodes and enables fast conversion kinetics.
In-situ Raman characterizations were performed to reveal the conversion mechanism of S cathodes in the 1M MAN electrolyte.

The pristine cathode shows obvious cathode particles on the surface (Figure 4b), and the corresponding Raman signals at 152, 217 and 472 cm1 all belong to S (Figure 4c).

As the discharge proceeds (40%), it generates solid species (without electrolyte signals as shown in Figure S7, Supporting Information) that mainly consists of Li2S8 on the cathode surface, as verified by new Raman signals at 402 and 455 cm1.
At a discharge state of 60%, it shows a continuous solid LPSs phase with Raman signals of Li2S8 and Li2S4–6 (200 cm1), and no S signals are detected.
At 100% discharge, all LPSs signals are absent from the Raman result, implying a complete conversion to Li2S.
More evidence of the solid conversion process is exhibited in Figure S8, Supporting Information, showing a continuous conversion from S particles to solid LPSs.
Subsequently, we conducted in-situ Raman characterizations on the evolution of LPSs content in electrolytes during discharge.
The in-situ cell configuration is illustrated in Figure 4d, with the laser being focused on the separator to detect the signal of separator-adsorbed electrolyte.

In-situ Raman results (Figure 4e) of the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte show high-intensity LPSs signals because the LPSs intermediates are prone to dissolve and diffuse in the highly solvating ether electrolyte.

With the 1M MAN electrolyte, in-situ Raman tests (Figure 4f) also detect LPSs signals during discharge, but the intensity is much lower than that in the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte, indicating the dissolution of LPSs is significantly suppressed owing to the low solubility of MAN to LPSs.
Combining the in-situ Raman characterizations on cathodes and electrolyte, it demonstrates a hybrid conversion process in the 1M MAN electrolyte with S converting to both solvated and solid LPSs.
The new conversion mechanism enabled by the MAN-based moderately solvating electrolyte could effectively decrease the E/S ratio and the porosity of the cathode.

With the 1M MAN electrolyte, Li-S batteries exhibit analogous discharge profiles (Figure 5a) under E/S ratios of 10, 5, 3, and 2 μL mg1, delivering high discharge capacities of 1038, 1043, 1070, and 1094 mAh g1, respectively.
In contrast, batteries with DOL/DME electrolyte suffer from a sharp capacity decay under lean electrolyte conditions (E/S ratio <5 μL mg1) (Figure 5b).
Moreover, the 1M MAN electrolyte is also compatible with calendared S cathodes.

Li-S batteries with porous cathodes represent an extremely low volumetric energy density, making it imperative to reduce the cathode porosity (detailed calculation in Table S3, Supporting Information).

Li-S batteries show regular discharge profiles in the 1M MAN electrolyte (Figure 5c) and deliver discharge capacities of 1066, 1060, 1063, and 958 mAh g1, respectively, with cathode porosities of 80%, 72%, 63%, and 52%, in comparison to low discharge capacities in the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte when the cathode porosity decreases to 63% and 52% (Figure 5d).
The working mechanism of S cathodes in the 1M MAN electrolyte under conditions of low E/S ratio and low porosity are illustrated, respectively, in Figure 5e,f.
During sulfur conversion in ether electrolytes, the high-LPSs-content catholyte significantly decreases Li+ conductivity and deteriorates wettability.

In contrast, 1M MAN electrolyte —with its “high dielectric constant (ε) and low donor number (DN)” design—provides sufficient free Li+ while moderately inhibiting LPSs dissolution to avoid electrolyte deterioration.

Therefore, S cathodes in 1M MAN electrolyte perform a hybrid conversion process (Figure 5e) with solid S to solvated LPSs, as well as solid S to solid LPSs, substantially reducing electrolyte involvement during redox reactions, ensuring a complete conversion under lean-electrolyte conditions.
Similarly, dense S cathodes are also capable to work at locally lean electrolyte conditions benefited from the unique S conversion mechanism in the 1M MAN electrolyte as shown in Figure 5f.
The practical prospect of Li-S batteries with the MAN electrolyte is further evaluated.

Under harsh conditions, with a low cathode porosity of 52% and a high area S loading of 4 mg cm2, the Li-S battery delivers a high initial discharge capacity of 907 mAh g1 and exhibits stable cycling for 50 cycles with 72% capacity retention (Figure 5g).

An Ah-level Li-S pouch cell (the inset photo in Figure S9, Supporting Information) is assembled with a calendared, high-S-content (68 wt%) and high-area-loading (7.4 mg cm2) cathode, a low E/S ratio of 2 μL mg1, and a thin Li foil with a thickness of 100 μm.
Detailed configuration of the Li-S pouch cell is displayed in Figure S10, Supporting Information.

The Li-S pouch cell shows the same two-plateau discharge profile (Figure S9, Supporting Information) as that in the coin cell and delivers a high discharge capacity of 1.13 Ah at 33.5 mA g1 with a total S loading of 1.18 g.
The 1.5 Ah-level pouch cell delivers a specific discharge capacity of 954 mAh g1 at 33.5 mA g1.

Conclusion In this work, we developed a moderately solvating MAN electrolyte to address the key issues (high electrolyte dosage and high cathode porosity) limiting the overall energy density of Li-S batteries.
MAN possesses a high relative permittivity but a low donor number, combining fast Li+ conductivity and suppressed dissolution to LPSs.

The 1M MAN electrolyte provides a unique conversion mechanism distinguished from that in highly solvating and sparingly solvating electrolytes, as revealed by in-situ Raman characterizations, with S converting to both solvated and solid LPSs.

The hybrid solid/solvating mechanism brings about fast conversion kinetics and avoids high-LPSs-content catholyte, as formed in the traditional DOL/DME-based electrolytes, which kinetically impedes the conversion process under lean and locally lean electrolyte conditions.

The 1M MAN electrolyte successfully enables S cathodes to run at an ultralow E/S ratio of 2 μL mg1 and a low cathode porosity of 52%, significantly boosting both gravimetric and volumetric energy density of Li-S batteries.
This work provides a methodology for developing electrolytes for high-energy-density Li-S batteries. 4.

Experimental Section Preparation of electrodes and electrolyte: S and Ketjen black (KB, ECP-600JD, Lion) in the mass ratio of 4:1 were first ground for 1 h to obtain a well-mixed S/KB mixture, which was then heated at 155 °C in an Argon atmosphere.

Sulfur cathode slurry was prepared by mixing S@KB composite, Super P (DodoChem), and LA133 binder (Chengdu Indigo Power Sources) at mass ratios of 80:12:8 (for the cathodes with 64 wt% S content) or 85:7:8 (for the cathodes with 68 wt% S content) in deionized water using a planetary centrifugal mixer (AR-100, THINKY) at 2000 rpm.
The cumulative mixing duration exceeded 30 min.
The resulting slurry was coated onto an aluminum foil current collector at a wet thickness of 400 μm to achieve an active material loading of 4 mg cm2.

For low-porosity cathodes (52% porosity), a freeze-drying process was employed: the as-prepared electrodes were frozen at 40 °C for 2 h followed by vacuum treatment at 0.1 Pa for 2 h to facilitate ice crystal sublimation.
All electrodes were vacuum dried at 60 °C for 10 h prior to use.

Dense sulfur cathodes were fabricated through calendering, where freeze-dried electrodes were repeatedly compressed at 60 °C using a hot roller system, with iterative reduction of the roller gap until the desired compacted thickness was achieved.
The 1M ether electrolyte was prepared by adding lithium bis(trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI, DoDoChem) into 1,3- dioxolane (DOL, 99%, DoDoChem) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, 99.5%, DoDoChem).
The 1M methoxyacetonitrile (MAN) electrolyte was prepared by first adding LiTFSI into MAN (Adamas) and then magnetically stirring for 1 h to obtain a clear solution.

The Diglyme (G2, 99.9%, Adamas)-based sparingly solvating electrolyte was prepared by first mixing LiTFSI and Diglyme in a 0.8:1 molar ratio and magnetically stirring at 60 °C for 12 h, then mixing the obtained LiTFSI/solvent solution with TTE in a 1:2 volume ratio.
Solubility test of LPSs: Excessive Li2S and S powder with a molar ratio of 1:5 were added into the DOL/DME mixture and MAN solvent.
The solutions were stirred at 600 r/min and at 60 °C for 48 h to obtain supersaturated Li2S6/solvent solutions, which were then centrifuged to obtain the supernatants.

Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, sourced from China National Pharmaceutical Group, Ltd.) and lithium hydroxide (LiOH, obtained from Adamas Reagent, Ltd.) were added into the supernatants to oxidize S2 x to SO2 4 .
Subsequently, barium chloride (BaCl2, Adamas Reagent, Ltd.) was introduced to precipitate barium sulfate (BaSO4).
The precipitate was collected by filtration, washed, dried, and then weighed.
The sulfur content was calculated based on the measured mass.

The wettability of electrolytes and LPSs-saturated electrolytes was evaluated by the contact angle of electrolytes on cathodes, which was measured on a contact angle surface analyzer (JC2000D1).
The porosity of S cathodes was measured on an automatic mercury porosimeter (MicroActive AutoPore V).
Samples weighing 0.5 g were cut to dimensions below 1 cm × 1 cm and placed in the sample chamber.
Mercury at 24.96 °C was then introduced into the chamber.
Pressure was subsequently applied to progressively force the mercury into the electrode structure, and the applied pressure range was 0.1–61 000 psia.
The contact angle was 130°.
The thickness of the electrode sample (hsam) and the current collector (hcur) were tested using a micrometer, and the coating thickness (hcoa) was subsequently calculated.

The electrode porosity without the current collector εcoa was calculated based on the sample porosity εsam using the following formula: εcoa = εsam 1 þ hcur hcoa   (1) Electrochemical tests: All cells were assembled in an Argon-filled glove box (Mikrouna) with O2 and H2O content below 0.01 ppm.
Coin cells consist of an S cathode (16 mm in diameter), a Li metal plate (16 mm in diameter), a separator (19 mm in diameter), and electrolyte.
The electrolyte dosage varied according to different E/S ratios.
The Ah-level Pouch cell was assembled as shown in Figure S10, Supporting Information.
The galvanostatic charge/discharge tests were performed on a Neware Battery test station at 25 °C.

We evaluated the performance of Li-S batteries with the traditional 1M DOL/DME electrolyte under practical conditions.
S1a shows an evaluated result of overall energy density of Li-S batteries at different E/S ratios.
Under an E/S ratio of 10 L mg−1, the mass ratio of the electrolyte is high to 77% for the Li-S battery (Fig.

S2a), and the available energy density is low to 174 Wh kg−1 (detailed calculation in Table S1 and S2), inferior to that of commercial LiFePO4 (LFP)-based (> 190 Wh kg−1) and LiNixMnyCo1−x−yO2 (NCM)-based (> 260 Wh kg−1) Li-ion batteries.
Even under an E/S ratio of 5 L mg−1 that is regarded as the threshold of lean electrolyte, the mass ratio of electrolyte is still high to 63% (Fig.
S2b), and the Li-S battery can only output an energy density of 283 Wh kg−1.
To meet the pursuit of energy density > 300 Wh kg−1, the E/S ratio must be decreased below to < 5 L mg−1.
However, Li-S batteries fail to work under such lean-electrolyte conditions.
The mechanism was revealed by our previous works [S1].
With high E/S ratios (Fig.
S1c), excessive electrolyte can fully dissolve LPSs intermediates and drive further reduction to Li2S2/Li2S.
While with low E/S ratios (Fig.

S1d), lean electrolyte transforms to a gel-like catholyte after dissolving a high content LPSs [S2, S3], and it undergoes a significant decrease in Li+ conductivity, along with severe deterioration in wettability to the cathode and the separator, which subsequently lead to the failure of the Li-S cell.
Besides, the 1M DOL/DME electrolyte demands high-porosity cathodes and thus leads to low volumetric energy density.
S1e shows that Li-S batteries with porous cathodes deliver much lower volumetric energy densities than commercial Li-ion batteries (detailed calculation in Table S3).

The failure mechanism is illustrated in Fig.

A dense cathode with limited pore volume only adsorbs a small amount of electrolyte within the electrode structure, and forms a locally low E/S ratio condition, which subsequently leads to cathode deterioration and battery failure.
